tier_reason: Upgraded from B to A. The paper (ESA 2025, arXiv v2) benchmarks against CMPH CHD, a category baseline, and states the CPU (Intel i7 11700), compiler (GCC 11.2.0) and flags (-O3 -march=native). The benchmark code is public in the repo: src/table.cpp (Table 2), src/comparison.cpp (Figure 5), contenders/ChdContender.hpp (cmph CHD through the extlib/cmph submodule) and scripts/table.sh.

corrections.baseline: CMPH CHD (cmph library, run as non-minimal k-perfect with load factor 0.97, because cmph CHD supports only non-minimal k-perfect hashing) and the ad-hoc threshold-based bumping kPHF from CONSENSUS-RecSplit [30]; no BBHash, PTHash or 1-perfect RecSplit comparison
corrections.workload: Minimal k-perfect hash function construction and queries for k = 10, 100 and 1000 on 100 million random strings of uniform random length in [10, 50]. Figure 5 plots space vs construction and query throughput; Table 2 lists representative configurations for k = 10 and k = 1000. There are no k = 1 (standard MPHF) experiments.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract: 'Our implementations simultaneously dominate older approaches in space consumption, construction time, and query time.' Table 2, k = 10: CHD (load factor 0.97) 0.627 bits/key, 495 ns/key construction, 96 ns/query; Threshold-Based 0.716 bits/key, 77 ns/key, 56 ns/query; Bucket Placement (Compact) 1.917 bits/key, 584 ns/key, 47 ns/query; Threshold-Based + Consensus 0.450 bits/key, 233 ns/key, 57 ns/query (better than CHD on all three). That is about 6.4x faster construction (Threshold-Based vs CHD) and 1.7x-2.0x faster queries (derived from page data). Text: up to 3 times smaller space overhead than the ad-hoc threshold-based implementation, and up to 50% faster construction than the next best technique. The CHD implementation crashes for k = 1000. Query times are 22-291 ns/query, not single-digit nanoseconds.
corrections.hardware: Intel i7 11700 (8 cores, 2.5 GHz base clock), Rocky Linux 9.5, Linux 5.14.0
corrections.caveats: ESA 2025 paper (LIPIcs vol. 351, 99:1-99:18, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2025.99; software artifact DOI 10.4230/artifacts.24698). This is a k-perfect hashing library (k = 10/100/1000 evaluated), not a 1-perfect MPHF. It is not compared against BBHash, PTHash or 1-perfect RecSplit. The only external baselines are cmph CHD, run non-minimal at load factor 0.97 and crashing at k = 1000, and the ad-hoc threshold-based bumping from CONSENSUS-RecSplit. CHD is slightly smaller than plain Threshold-Based at k = 10 (0.627 vs 0.716 bits/key), but Threshold-Based + Consensus beats CHD on space, construction and query. Table 2 is plain text in the PDF, not images. GPL-3.0 applies.

notes: The original claimed_speedup was substantially wrong. It said k = 1 single-digit-ns queries with explicit BBHash/PTHash/RecSplit/CHD comparisons, but the paper has no k = 1 experiments and compares only against cmph CHD and the ad-hoc threshold-based bumping. The corrected claim uses Table 2. The claim was overstated, but the tier went up (B to A) because the code, compiler, flags and CPU are all present. The last commit on master (the only branch) is 2025-07-03; pushed_at is 2025-11-13 but has no newer commit, so the status is stale (about 14.7 months).

tier_reason: The only rust-phf-specific number is first-party, from conduit-mime-types PR #18: Types::new() 'now runs in 3ns instead of 300ms'. The PR gives no hardware, compiler or methodology, and the Criterion bench (benches/load-data.rs) was deleted in that same PR. The gain is implausible (about 10^8x) and the flags are unstated, so the tier is capped at C.

corrections.baseline: std::collections::HashMap (Rust) populated at runtime from statically bundled (code-generated) data
corrections.workload: Initializing conduit-mime-types' extension-to-MIME-type and MIME-type-to-extension lookup tables (Types::new()). Before PR #18, statically bundled, code-generated data was inserted into two std::collections::HashMap at runtime; JSON parsing had already moved to development time in PR #17. After PR #18, phf_codegen in build.rs emits two compile-time phf maps, so initialization is essentially empty.
corrections.claimed_speedup: PR #18 (Turbo87, merged 2021-10-11): with rust-phf generating both lookup tables at build time, Types::new() becomes 'an essentially empty function' that 'now runs in 3ns instead of 300ms' (first-party, no methodology). The Mainmatter post's 'roughly 80% performance improvement' belongs to the earlier code-generation step (PR #17, which still filled HashMaps at runtime), not to rust-phf. For the rust-phf step, the post says only that initialization time dropped to 'essentially zero' and that lookups got faster, with no numbers.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 2,193 stars; used by conduit-mime-types, a crates.io server dependency according to the 2022 Mainmatter post (the conduit-mime-types repo is now archived)
corrections.caveats: The numbers are a first-party anecdote from a PR description (3ns vs 300ms for Types::new()) with no hardware, compiler or timing methodology. The comparison moves work from run time to compile time; it does not compare lookup speed. The Mainmatter blog (Tobias Bieniek, 2022-06-23) gives no numbers for the rust-phf step. Its 80% figure is for the earlier codegen step, which does not use rust-phf. There is no comparison against C++ std::unordered_map or gperf; the comparison is Rust-only. The repo has a phf-vs-HashMap/BTreeMap/match microbenchmark (phf_macros_test/benches/bench.rs, nightly #[bench]) but no published results.

notes: The record misattributed the Mainmatter '80%' figure to rust-phf; it belongs to the pre-phf codegen step (PR #17). The corrected benchmark_url points to PR #18, which has the only phf-specific number. That number is '3ns instead of 300ms', quoted verbatim. The 300ms unit looks suspicious after PR #17's 80% cut but could not be checked, so it is left as written. The tier stays at C and the metadata (MIT, 2026-09-17, active, not a fork) is confirmed.
